bib.title: A large annotated corpus for learning natural language inference
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 2015 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pages 632-642

question: Can a large, human-written, grounded corpus of sentence pairs enable learned (lexicalized and neural) models to do natural language inference competitively?
hypothesis: A corpus two orders of magnitude larger and of high quality will make parameter-rich models such as neural networks competitive at NLI.
contributions: SNLI corpus: 570,152 human-written sentence pairs labeled entailment/neutral/contradiction via a grounded image-caption task
Validation of 56,951 pairs with five labels each
Evaluation of EOP, lexicalized classifier and sum/RNN/LSTM sentence-embedding models
Transfer of the SNLI LSTM to SICK

method.summary: Crowdworkers on Mechanical Turk wrote three hypotheses (entailment, neutral, contradiction) for each Flickr30k caption shown without its image; about 10% of pairs were validated by four extra annotators. Baselines and models (EOP, feature classifier, 100d sum/RNN/LSTM sentence encoders plus 3x200d tanh classifier) were trained and tested on it, and the LSTM transferred to SICK.
method.task: natural language inference (3-class: entailment, neutral, contradiction)

datasets.name: SNLI
datasets.split: 550,152 train / 10,000 dev / 10,000 test; each Flickr caption in only one split; dev and test fully validated
datasets.source: Premises: Flickr30k captions (about 160k captions, about 30k images); hypotheses written by about 2,500 MTurk workers; about 4k pilot pairs use VisualGenome premises (train only, ids prefixed vg); CC BY-SA
datasets.preprocessing: Parsed with Stanford PCFG Parser 3.5.2 trained on standard training set plus Brown Corpus; images not used; pairs without 3-of-5 consensus get label '-' and are excluded from experiments

models.name: 100d sum of words
models.architecture: sum of word embeddings, 300d GloVe mapped by tanh layer to 100d

models.name: 100d LSTM RNN
models.architecture: LSTM sentence encoder, two copies; outputs concatenated into 3 stacked 200d tanh layers and 3-way softmax

models.name: Lexicalized classifier
models.architecture: linear classifier, 6 feature types (BLEU 1-4, length diff, overlap, hypothesis uni/bigrams, cross-unigrams, cross-bigrams)

models.name: EOP edit distance / classifier
models.architecture: Excitement Open Platform algorithms, optionally with WordNet and VerbOcean

training.objective: 3-class classification (softmax), sentence encoder and classifier trained jointly
training.lr_schedule: AdaDelta adaptive; for SICK transfer the AdaDelta accumulators are carried over, lowering starting rates
training.dropout: applied to inputs and outputs of the sentence embedding models (not internal connections), fixed rate (value not given)
training.regularisation: L2 with manually tuned lambda per model (values not given)

other.transfer: SICK transfer initialises from SNLI LSTM; only softmax and new-word embeddings are new; same hyperparameters except L2 re-tuned

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: 3-class accuracy on test set; 2-class for EOP (contradiction and unknown merged to non-entailment)

metrics.name: Fleiss kappa
metrics.definition: agreement over validated examples with five annotations

eval.protocol: Single reported runs, no seeds or significance tests; LSTM accuracy varies up to 0.5% between evaluation steps near stopping iteration.

availability.code: Implementations 'will be made available at publication time' (no URL)

prompts.text: We will show you the caption for a photo. We will not show you the photo. Using only the caption and what you know about the world: Write one alternate caption that is definitely a true description of the photo. ... might be a true description of the photo. ... definitely a false description of the photo.

results.claim: SNLI has 570,152 sentence pairs, two orders of magnitude larger than other NLI resources.
results.quote: At 570,152 sentence pairs, SNLI is two orders of magnitude larger than all other resources of its type.

results.claim: 100d LSTM sentence-embedding model reaches 77.6% test accuracy on SNLI 3-class.
results.setup: SNLI test set, 3-class, 550,152 train pairs; 100d LSTM RNN, GloVe 840B init, 3x200d tanh classifier
results.table: Table 6, row 100d LSTM RNN, column Test (77.6)

results.claim: Lexicalized feature classifier reaches 78.2% test accuracy (99.7% train) on SNLI 3-class.
results.setup: SNLI test set, 3-class, 550,152 train pairs; BLEU, length, overlap, unigram/bigram, cross-unigram, cross-bigram features
results.note: Train accuracy 99.7 shows near-perfect fit of training set

results.claim: Unlexicalized features alone give 50.4% test accuracy on SNLI, far above lexicalized gain (78.2%).
results.setup: SNLI test set, 3-class, 550,152 train pairs; features 1-3 only

results.claim: Sum-of-words baseline 75.3% test, plain RNN 72.2% test.
results.setup: SNLI test set, 3-class, 550,152 train pairs; 100d sum of words (RNN 72.2)
results.table: Table 6, row 100d Sum of words, column Test (75.3); row 100d RNN Test (72.2)

results.claim: Transferring SNLI-trained LSTM to SICK gives 80.8% test accuracy vs 71.3% from SICK alone.
results.setup: SICK 3-class test; LSTM initialised from SNLI-trained params, AdaDelta accumulators also transferred, L2 re-tuned
results.table: Table 7, row Our data and SICK (transfer), column Test (80.8)

results.claim: Model trained on SNLI only gets 46.7% on SICK test (domain/label-presentation mismatch).
results.setup: SICK test, LSTM trained only on SNLI
results.table: Table 7, row Our data only, column Test (46.7)

results.claim: State of the art on SICK at the time was 84.6% and interannotator agreement 84%.
results.quote: approaches both the overall state of the art at 84.6% (Lai and Hockenmaier, 2014) and the 84% level of interannotator agreement

results.note: Intro prints 56,941 validated examples and 58%; Table 3 prints 56,951 and 58.3%
results.table: Table 3, row Pairs w/ unanimous gold label (58.3%)

results.setup: Validated pairs with full five annotations

results.claim: Individual annotator label equals gold label 89.0% of the time.
results.table: Table 3, row Individual label = gold label (89.0%)

results.claim: Gold label equals the author's label for 91.2% of validated pairs; 2.0% have no gold label.
results.table: Table 3, row Gold label = author's label (91.2%)

results.claim: Edit-distance EOP baseline gets 71.9% 2-class on SNLI; classifier+lexical resources 75.0%.
results.setup: 2-class (contradiction/neutral merged to non-entailment); most-frequent-class baseline 66% SNLI
results.table: Table 4, row + Lexical Resources, column SNLI (75.0)

results.claim: Premise mean length 14.1 tokens, hypothesis 8.3 tokens; 37,026 distinct words.
results.table: Table 2, row Premise mean token count (14.1); hypothesis 8.3; distinct words 37,026

results.claim: About 2,500 crowd workers contributed; premises from about 160k Flickr30k captions (about 30k images).
Lexicalized classifier with only 100 training examples already beats the unlexicalized one; learning curve shows corpus size is crucial and LSTM slope is steeper.
results.setup: Fig 4 learning curve, 1 to 1,000,000 training pairs, log scale, LSTM minibatch 64 sets lower bound on its data

limits: Authors concede a full comparison of classifier-based NLI approaches awaits future work: only models that scale to SNLI unmodified were evaluated.
Sentence-embedding models cannot compare premise and hypothesis at word/phrase level (by design); stronger interaction models excluded.
Coreference indeterminacy is mitigated, not solved; labels depend on a caption-grounded scenario.
Models fail on world knowledge, lexical relations (beach/surf), and role-reversal cases (A soup bowl prepares a woman).
Transfer to RTE-3 failed (800 training examples too few).
Hyperparameters (L2, dropout rate, learning rate, epochs) and seeds not reported.
Lexicalized model overfits train (99.7 vs 78.2). Later work (not in paper) found hypothesis-only artifacts; not claimed here.
